A B S T R A C T

Marine accident investigation reports contain valuable vet underutilized information due to their unstructured nature. While knowledge graphs (KGs) offer a promising solution for structured modeling and quantitative reasoning based on these reports, the construction of high-quality, domain-specific KGs remains technically challenging. To enable more efficient and scalable knowledge extraction in maritime safety domain, this study proposes an automated pipeline based on large language models (LLMs) which enhances existing approaches by customizing LLM prompting and evaluation frameworks. A chain-of-thought and one-shot prompting method is adopted to identify critical hazardous factors and their coupling relationships. Besides, a comprehensive quality assessment framework is developed to assess the accuracy and complexity of the generated KGs. Applied to realworld accident reports from maritime authorities, the proposed LLM-based method demonstrates substantial improvements in automation efficiency and extraction accuracy compared with traditional approaches. Furthermore, the quality evaluation framework provides complementary indicators to traditional metrics by reflecting the global semantic coherence and structural redundancy of the maritime safety KG. The findings offei actionable insights for deploying LLM-based tools to support data-driven maritime risk analysis enhancing transport safety management and decision making in complex operational environments.
1. Introduction

Maritime transport safety is influenced by a complex interplay of factors, including adverse weather conditions, vessel defects, human error, and operational mismanagement (Rawson et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2022). The occurrences of marine accidents are often characterized by uncertainty, and can result in severe consequences, affecting lives, as sets, and the environment (Shu et al., 2025; Siqueira et al., 2022). Consequently, such accidents are typically sparsely and irregularly recorded over time and documented in unstructured formats with high-dimensional representations for post-incident analysis (i.e., acci dent investigation reports). While these reports contain rich informa tion, their narrative style and domain-specific language pose significant challenges to effective data utilization (Yan et al., 2023).

To address these challenges, knowledge graphs (KGs) have emerged as a promising solution for modeling marine accident process by trans forming unstructured text into structured semantic networks. They are able to support the identification of causal chains, control and mitiga tion of risk propagation, and prediction of the hazardous events (Liu et al., 2025). However, developing high-quality, domain-specific KGs remains a labor-intensive task. It demands significant domain expertise in both maritime operations and technical language interpretation, making it difficult to scale across large accident report collections.

Recent advances in generative large language models (LLMs) have opened new possibilities for automating this process. With the powerful capabilities of semantic understanding and logical reasoning, LLMs can perform key tasks, such as named entity recognition (NER) and relation extraction (Wang et al., 2023; Dagdelen et al., 2024). Yet, the applica tion of LLMs in maritime safety contexts is still in its infancy. Moreover, their outputs are prone to pitfalls (e.g., hallucination, inconsistent cor eference, and omission of critical context), potentially compromising the validity of the resulting KGs.

This paper addresses these challenges by investigating how LLMs can be effectively employed for automated knowledge extraction based on marine accident investigation reports from the United Kingdom (1990–2023) and China (2016–2024). This paper also investigates how to evaluate and optimize the quality of the generated KG. Ultimately, the proposed KG construction and evaluation framework is expected to enable scalable analysis of large volumes of marine accident reports and support systematic identification of risk factors to enhance safety in the maritime transport domain. 2. Literature review
2.1. Marine accident analysis with knowledge graphs

Marine accidents are influenced by dynamic meteorological condi tions (e.g., winds, waves and low visibility), vessel inherent defects, and operational or management failures (Luo et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2025). These incidents are often low in frequency but high in consequence (Chen, P. et al., 2022). Compared to other operational data, the accident records are sparse and predominantly unstructured, posing challenges for traditional accident analytical models such as Fault Tree Analysis (FTA) and Bayesian Network (BN) that demonstrate limitations in semantical representation and nuanced information storage (Li et al. 2024; Xiong et al., 2024). To address these issues, KGs have emerged as a promising approach for marine accident analysis.

KGs represent complex systems through networks of heterogeneous entities, attributes, and relations, making them particularly well-suited for modeling multi-factorial causes and cascading effects (Zarei et al., 2022). To accurately represent the marine accident process, customized concepts and entity types must be defined in addition to the general entity types (e.g., person, location, time, and organizations) used in open-domain tasks (Barron et al., 2024). For instance, Gan et al. (2023) developed an ontology of ship collision accidents integrating context-based and content-based metadata. Contextual elements, such as accident descriptions, responsibility, and administrative advice, were incorporated to preserve the original information of reports, while content elements including involved ships, location, causes and conse quences, were identified to reflect multi-dimensional perspective of the accidents. Attributes of entities, such as the numerical hazard severity level and the enumerated event types, were used to provide structured variability across standardized entities (Zhu et al., 2024). As for re lations, causal and spatial-temporal relationships are crucial in accident causation modeling. Xie et al. (2024) employed causal and sequential relations to link the vessel events and actions. Huang et al. (2025) constructed causal chains to capture the causal and temporal dynamics of event evolution in railway accidents.

By encoding the above elements into graphs, KGs transform unstructured narratives into machine-readable, semantically rich for mats while preserving much of the original contextual details. Despite the promise, challenges remain in constructing high-quality domainspecific KGs due to the complexity of unstructured texts rich in technical terms (Liu et al., 2023). The time-intensive nature of knowledge extraction along with the high cost of expert annotation, continues to hinder their widespread application in maritime safety management.
2.2. Knowledge graph construction methods for the marine accident domain

A typical KG in the marine accident domain consists of two layers: a schema layer defining the conceptual structure and a data layer where case-specific information is instantiated (Zhang et al., 2019). Two pri mary ways of constructing KGs are employed: (1) top-down: an ontology is defined as the schema first and then used to guide knowledge extraction; (2) bottom-up: KG elements are extracted from data without schema constraints and then followed by schema abstraction. In do mains with well-established domain knowledge, such as maritime safety, the top-down method enables the systematic formalization of existing expertise into reusable ontologies, thereby facilitating struc tured knowledge extraction and reasoning, while the bottom-up method is widely applied in open-domain KGs (Chen, T. et al., 2022).

Schema design in the maritime context is heavily dependent on domain expertise, requiring accurate definitions of entities, relations, and constraints unique to shipping operations and accident causation (Zhou et al., 2022). In contrast, the information extraction process, typically involving entity recognition and relation extraction, follows a more standardized pipeline. In the studies by Liu et al. (2024) and Huo et al. (2024), domain-specific KGs were constructed for the accident analysis in railway operations and construction sectors through a pipeline-based extraction approach. These works laid important foun dations for structured knowledge representation in specific domains, although the extraction process still relied primarily on manual anno tation and rule-based methods. With the growing volume of multi-source marine accident reports, there is an increasing need for automated, scalable, and robust information extraction techniques (Zhong et al., 2023). Deep learning and statistical learning models have exhibited satisfying performance in automated NER and relation extraction tasks. For instance, Liu and Cheng (2024) combined Bidi rectional Encoder Representation from Transformer (BERT), Bidirec tional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM), conditional random fields, and a self-training strategy to develop a maritime-specific NER model that achieved satisfying performance. However, these enhanced pre-trained models often require annotated corpora and domain-specific retraining, limiting their adaptability and scalability. To alleviate the effort of annotation, unsupervised methods such as topic model have been applied in extracting structured knowledge from open-ended texts (Baburajan et al., 2022). Yet, such models may fall short in capturing complex event structures or semantic relationships.

Recent advancements in generative LLMs provide a promising alternative. By reframing KG construction as sequence-to-sequence structure prediction task, LLMs can better comprehend complex taskrelated knowledge with multi-head self-attention mechanisms (Ye et al., 2022). LLMs have been successfully prompted to carry out open-domain KG construction under Wikidata schema without anno tated data (Feng et al., 2024; Abolhasani and Pan, 2024). Moreover, LLM-generated KGs serve as foundational components in advanced retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) techniques, such as GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) and knowledge-augmented generation (Liang et al., 2025). Beyond KG construction, LLMs have also demonstrated strong capabilities in bridging semantic understanding with physical reasoning in complex transportation systems (Liu et al., 2025). Given the complexity and domain-specific language of marine accident data, which includes technical terminology and regulatory references, manual KG construction and data annotation remain costly and inefficient. Thi motivates the exploration of LLM-based KG construction for maritime safety analysis.

2.3. Quality assessment of domain knowledge graphs

Quality assessment of the developed KG is of significant necessity for ensuring its reliability and utility in downstream tasks. While manual evaluation remains the most accurate approach in theory, it is resourceintensive, non-scalable, and unsuitable for benchmarking across algo rithms or large-scale datasets (Qi et al., 2022; Si et al., 2024).

One common strategy is the partial gold standard approach, where a subset of data is selected as test set and manually labeled to calculate standard metrics such as F1 score and area under curve (AUC) for knowledge extraction quality evaluation (Paulheim, 2016). However, this approach only assesses extraction accuracy and fails to capture broader dimensions of KG quality. To address this, scholars have extended general data quality measurement (i.e., intrinsic, contextual, representation, and accessibility) to KG quality evaluation (Xue and Zou, 2022). Besides, the structure and path characteristics of KG bring additional possibilities of developing dedicated dimensions and metrics. Metrics regarding abundant sub-division of ontology hierarchy, the number of attributes per class, class diversity, and overall graph complexity have been proposed in existing studies (Seo et al., 2022).

Despite various frameworks being proposed, many are either overly complex for practical use or lack scalability for large-scale KGs (Chen et al., 2019). Moreover, effective evaluation should be grounded in the domain-specific use cases. In marine accident analysis, particular emphasis should by placed on verifying the completeness and retriev ability of triggering factors and risk propagation paths, which are central to safety diagnostics and causation modeling (Ma et al., 2022). Another concern is that the LLM-based knowledge extraction may introduce extra quality risks, such as hallucinated facts, coreference errors, and missing context. These risks highlight the need for assessment methods capable of detecting semantic inconsistence and verifying the fidelity of the extracted knowledge against the original text (Zhang et al., 2024).
2.4. Research gap and workflow

Despite growing interest in developing KGs for marine accident analysis, few automated methods have been tailored to handle the un structured, technical, and narrative-heavy nature of accident reports. While recent advance in generative LLMs brings potential for schemaguided extraction, their application in the maritime safety domain re mains underexplored. Based on the above review, three key research gaps are identified:
(1) The development of automated pipelines specifically tailored for structuring information from marine accident reports remains underexplored.

(2) Establishing a comprehensive and scalable quality assessment framework remains an important need for assessing the quality of domain-specific KGs and advancing their applications in the context of marine accident analysis.
(3) The impact of key configuration choices, such as decoding pa rameters, schema, and prompt design, on the quality of LLMgenerated KGs has not been fully investigated.

To address these gaps, this study proposes an LLM-based framework for automated KG construction and quality assessment in marine acci dent analysis. The construction pipeline applies chain-of-thought and few-shot prompting strategies to guide the LLM to identify the entities and relations, and employs encoding model to generate embeddings for the extracted knowledge. In terms of evaluation, a dual-perspective framework is introduced. Complexity metrics assess whether the struc tural richness of the KG contributes meaningful insights for marine ac cident analysis. The accuracy assessment relies on LLM-aided text reconstruction and textual similarity scoring to evaluate the faithfulness of KG. By using these metrics, this study further explores the influencing factors and risks of LLM-based KG construction based on comparison analysis across various configuration settings on real-world marine ac cident corpora.
3. Methodology
3.1. Methodological framework

The proposed framework for constructing and evaluating a KG in the maritime safety management domain is illustrated in Fig. 1. It comprises four core modules, which are data collection, schema construction, KG generation, and KG quality assessment. This study primarily focuses on the application of LLMs to the KG construction and quality assessment processes.

First, marine accident data are sourced from official web-source databases provided and maintained by maritime authorities. The raw textual records are preprocessed and segmented into text chunks in a customized corpus for safety knowledge extraction. The chunks serve as inputs of the KG generation module.

Second, schema design is a critical prerequisite for KG development. It defines the scope of domain knowledge by specifying marine-and safety related concepts and identifying potential entity and relation types. The schema provides structural guidance to the LLMs during knowledge extraction, enabling consistent and domain-aware outputs.

Third, the process of knowledge extraction is decomposed into a series of sub-tasks. Each sub-task is handled by a generative LLM (KG extractor) with task-specific prompt engineering. Based on the text chunks and schema, the model outputs subject-predicate-object (SPO) triplets, which are stored and visualized in a graph database. Moreover, their vector representations are generated by an embedding LLM (KG encoder) and stored in vector database to facilitate downstream tasks.

Fourth, a dual-perspective assessment framework for maritime safety management KG is proposed in terms of complexity and accuracy. Complexity evaluation focuses on identifying redundancy in entities, relations, and graph structure, ensuring the KG remains concise and free of trivial or unnecessary components. Redundancy refers to the presence of semantically equivalent entities, invalid or duplicated relations, and excessive structural elements that contribute little meaningful infor mation to the knowledge graph (Zhong et al., 2023). To assess accuracy, a novel evaluation approach based on text reconstruction and semantic similarity analysis is introduced. A generative LLM (text reconstructor) is prompted to regenerate textual descriptions from sub-graphs corre sponding to individual accident records. Semantic similarity between the original and reconstructed text chunks serves as a proxy for the fi delity of the KG. The assessment results guide iterative refinements to the schema and prompt templates, facilitating continuous improvement of KG quality in maritime safety management applications.

These un structured textual records often involve intricate relationships between entities and hazardous events, making them a valuable source for safety risk analysis. In this study, a domain-specific corpus by focusing on weather related marine accident reports is established and sourced from 172 MAIB reports (from 1990 to 2023) and 33 MSA reports (from 2016 to 2024). These two databases are selected due to their high-quality documentation and the ability to filter reports by keywords or acci dent category labels, which facilitates the identification of relevant re ports. This choice of focusing on weather-related accidents is driven by both methodological and practical considerations. Methodologically, although the dataset coverage is limited. the designed schema still captures multiple causal dimensions including vessel characteristics, human factors, and operational contexts, which allows the framework to process diverse types of entities and relations in other maritime accident scenarios. Moreover. weather-related cases usually exhibit more uniform causal chains and more consistent contextual semantics, which facilitate precise schema design and enhance the LLM's extraction accuracy. Practically, extreme maritime weather has demonstrated sig nificant impact on safety risk in recent years, underscoring the urgent need for action by the shipping and ocean communities (Brandt et al., 2024). Weather-related marine accidents are identified through abstract screening and keyword filtering. Relevant paragraphs describing acci dent summaries and causative analyses are collected to form the domain-specific corpus for KG development. A more detailed descrip tion of the MAIB and MSA datasets is provided in Section 4.

In the chunk split stage, each selected accident report is segmented into a single chunk representing the complete context of an individual accident. This design ensures that all extracted entities and relations within a chunk are semantically and contextually linked to the same case. By maintaining the integrity of accident-level context during knowledge extraction, the approach reduces the risk of cross-record semantic interference and enhances the accuracy and traceability of downstream KG construction and evaluation.
3.3. Schema construction

The KG schema is designed to model the structural and causal logic of weather-related marine accidents, supporting downstream applications, such as risk pattern induction, responsibility identification, and resilience-oriented decision-making. The construction process follows a problem-driven and ontology-informed approach comprising the following five key steps.
(1) Objective Definition

The objective of the schema is to formalize key elements of weatherrelated marine accidents via the 5W1H framework (who, where, when, what, why/how) in a comprehensive and machine-interpretable form (Yang et al., 2011). The schema is hierarchically designed to incorporate the domain-relevant concepts, entity types, and relations. Table 1 pre sents the correspondence between schema elements and the 5W1H dimensions.
(2) Concept Layer Design

Top-level concepts (Vessel, Time, Location, Weather, HazardousEvent, and Accident) are identified through expert analysis of representative accident reports. These concepts serve as semantic anchors for defining subordinate entity types, thereby enhancing interpretability and struc tural clarity.
(3) Entity Type Specification

Subclasses of core concepts are organized as entity types based on frequently occurring elements in marine accident reports. For instance, ShipName, ShipType, Cargo, and ShipOperation are grounded under the concept of Vessel. For entity types with multiple but bounded categories, such as ShipOperation, ShipResponse, ContributingFactor, and AccidentE vent, enumerated attributes are introduced to standardize their ranges and reduce linguistic variability. The relations are specified as SPO triplets as shown in the fourth column of Table 1. These relations are defined to capture both static and dynamic aspects of maritime operations and accidents. Static facts describe inherent properties of vessels (e.g., hasTypeOf, carry). Dynamic relations reflect the time-varying weather conditions and operational contexts (e.g., characterizedBy, engagedInOperation, exhibitedResponse). Spatial and temporal anchors (e.g., occurredOn, occurredAt) are intro duced to provide contextual alignment with time and location of the dynamic events. The causal relations (e.g., cause) explicitly model the accident progression with causal chains, allowing the KG to represent the accident evolution paths among weather conditions, ship responses, contributing factors, and accident consequences.
(5) Schema Formatting

Given its role as a key input to LLMs, the schema should be both human-readable and parseable by machines. Thus, it is organized by JSON format in this study, which facilitates iterative schema refinement, programmatic manipulation and compatibility with LLM prompts. A preliminary schema for extracting weather-related marine accident knowledge is presented in Appendix A.
3.4. Knowledge graph generation

An automated pipeline for knowledge extraction and KG develop ment is proposed with the aid of LLMs and alongside programmatic controls. Considering the complexity of knowledge extraction, it is decomposed into a series of sub-tasks: NER, entity standardization, and relation extraction, with each step handled by LLMs. This design im proves the extraction reliability by simplifying the prompt in each step to avoid the distraction of LLM (Hwang et al., 2025). Besides, it enables stepwise quality control and optimization, in line with the principles of chain-of-thought.
3.4.1. Named entity recognition

NER aims to identify elements involved in each accident record. A one-shot prompt is designed to guide the generative LLM, referred to as the KG extractor, to extract entities and their attributes in accordance with the schema constraints. The prompt includes role and context in structions, the extraction schema, an annotated example, and output formatting requirements. An example of NER prompt is provided in Appendix B.
3.4.2. Entity standardization

Variability in the entity naming across documents may lead to redundancy of entities, negatively impacting the scale of KG, the calculation efficiency, and relation extraction accuracy. To address this issue, it is necessary to transform the entity mentions into normalized forms. The KG extractor is prompted to map overly specific terms to standardized equivalents (e.g., timestamps, measurement units, and common hazardous events). An example standardization prompt is included in Appendix B.
3.4.3. Relation extraction

The final step in the extraction pipeline involves identifying the SPO triplets among extracted entities, where the relation types are strictly in consistent with the scheme. Emphasis is placed on producing wellstructured JSON output, with instructions to validate and, if needed, revise the result. Appendix B includes a sample prompt for relation extraction.
3.4.4. LLM decoding parameter configuration

In addition to prompting, the LLM performance is also influenced by decoding parameters, which should be specified to control the randomness and diversity of the outputs when calling LLM. Specifically, this study tunes two parameters, temperature and top-p, to balance the determinism and variability of LLM outputs in knowledge extraction. A higher temperature setting promotes more diverse outputs, whereas a lower one yields more deterministic results (Renze, 2024). The top-p parameter constrains the token sampling to high-probability candidate tokens, thereby enhancing output stability and stylistic consistency (Holtzman et al., 2019). Detailed definitions of these two parameters are provided in Appendix C.
3.4.5. Embedding

The purpose of embeddings is to provide a continuous and computable representation of the extracted knowledge, enabling quan titative operations that cannot be directly performed on symbolic graph elements. Textual contents are converted into semantic vectors by an embedding LLM (referred to as KG encoder) and stored within the database. As a crucial component of the developed KG, the embedding enable its quality assessment and other downstream applications. In KG evaluation, the embeddings are applied to identify entity redundancy in complexity assessment and quantify semantic fidelity of extracted trip lets in accuracy evaluation. Beyond quality assessment, they also facil itate semantic retrieval in knowledge-based RAG systems, allowing the identification of conceptually related information that may not be directly linked in the graph structure.

3.5. Knowledge graph quality assessment

To ensure the reliability and utility of KG generated by LLMs, a comprehensive quality assessment framework is proposed. The KG is assessed in dual aspects: complexity and accuracy. Complexity evaluates the degree of conciseness and structural efficiency of the KG, assessing whether entities, relations, and overall graph structure are represented in a minimal but sufficient form to enclose the underlying knowledge. Accuracy, on the other hand, measures the fidelity of the KG to the original text, evaluating whether the graph correctly captures the key information expressed in the source material. These dimensions reflect a trade-off where reduced complexity supports computational efficiency and interpretability in downstream tasks while excessive simplification may lead to the loss of critical information. Accordingly, quantitative indices are developed to guide the optimization of KG construction.
3.5.1. Complexity assessment
The complexity is primarily assessed through the redundancy of extracted entities, relations, and the graph structure.
(1) Entity Redundancy Rate

Entity redundancy is defined as the presence of multiple entities in the KG that describe the same or highly similar instances (e.g., “strong winds” and “high winds”) leading to unnecessary duplication in the graph representation. Despite the implementation of entity standardi zation, some semantically equivalent entities may still occur due to the linguistic variability in accident reports. To assess the degree of entity redundancy, a clustering method is employed to group potentially equivalent entities as presented in Appendix D. The entity redundancy rate is defined as the proportion of entities that belong to multi-member clusters of equivalence.
(2) Relation Redundancy Rate

Two types of relation redundancy are considered, which are multiple relations between the same entity pair and self-loops where the head and tails of SPO triplets are identical. These relations violate the schema constraints and reduce the graph clarity. The relation redundancy rate is calculated as the ratio of redundant relations to the total number of relations.
(3) Graph Structure Complexity

To assess whether the developed graph contains redundant or un necessarily complex structures representing subordinate information in marine accident reports, a graph-entropy measure is introduced. Graph information entropy is a quantitative measure of the structural disorder and information dispersion within a graph, derived from the probability distribution of node degrees or connection strengths. A higher entropy value indicates a more complex graph structure reflecting a greater dispersion of information across nodes and relations. In this study, a main causal chain is first defined, encompassing essential relations that characterize the causation of weather-related marine accidents (e.g., “causes”, “exhibitedResponse”, “engagedInOperation”). Then, the graph information entropy of the main causal chain is compared with that of the corresponding accident-specific KG sub-graph to evaluate whether the structural complexity required to describe the main causal chain dominates the overall sub-graph. The mathematical definition of graph information entropy is presented in Appendix E.
3.5.2. Accuracy assessment

It is a significant challenge to evaluate the semantic faithfulness of the KG against the original text due to the lack of ground truth and the inherent ambiguity in language. In this study, an LLM-based text reconstruction method is proposed to address this issue.

The extracted SPO triplets of each marine accident report are incorporated into a prompt and fed into a generative LLM (the text reconstructor) to reconstruct a complete narrative of the accident process. An example prompt for text reconstruction is presented in Ap pendix B.

text: To accurately assess the semantic alignment of generated and orig inal chunks, a sentence-level similarity assessment approach is con ducted (Fig. 2). Both chunks are segmented into sentences. For each sentence in the original chunk, the highest similarity score with any sentence in the generated chunk is recorded. The average value of these maximum scores is adopted as the ultimate similarity measure. This approach mitigates the influence of word ordering, syntactic variation, and structural mismatch, especially in scenarios where the recon structed text reorganizes content without changing its core meaning.

A bi-encoder model is applied to provide more robust sentence-level embeddings in the similarity assessment as presented in Fig. 2. In this framework, two input sentences are encoded independently using a shared BERT encoder. Each sentence embedding is obtained by applying a pooling operation over the token embeddings from the final BERT layer. The resulting fixed-size vectors can then be compared using cosine similarity to estimate semantic closeness (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) Compared to cross-encoder models, bi-encoder models are less affected by reordering or paraphrasing, making them better suited for this evaluation setting, where semantic inclusion and coverage are the pri mary goals (Thakur et al., 2020).
4. Knowledge graph construction and assessment
4.1. Marine accident investigation report data source

This study utilizes weather-related marine accident investigation reports collected from two authoritative sources: the MAIB in the U.K. and the MSA in China. The focus on weather-related cases is inten tionally chosen to maintain the contextual consistency across samples and to emphasize the environmental dimension of accident causation. A detailed justification for this dataset scope has been provided in Section 3.2.

(1) MAIB reports. The MAIB reports marine accidents involving UKregistered vessels worldwide and all vessels operating in the UK territorial waters. From a total of 1067 reports, 172 weatherrelated cases from 1990 to 2023 are selected via keywords such as “weather”, “heavy weather”, and “rough sea”. The MAIB pro vides detailed investigation report in PDF format as well as websource summary of key findings and safety issues. To accommo date the input length constraints of LLMs and minimize pre processing complexity, the more concentrated web-source information is extracted by web scraping techniques and used to develop the MAIB corpus.

(2) China MSA reports. The China MSA reports marine accidents occurring in both coastal and inland waters in China. Among the officially defined categories, reports in “strong wind-induced accidents” from 2016 to 2024 are selected for this case. All 33 investigation reports in this category are included. As MSA re ports are only available in detailed investigation files, relevant sections of accident descriptions and causation analysis are manually extracted to form the second corpus.

Two corpora are processed independently and fed into the KG con struction pipeline to verify the robustness and generalizability of the framework across different reporting styles and languages. Summary statistics of the two datasets are provided in Table 2.
4.2. Weather-related marine accident knowledge graph construction

The schema described in Appendix A and the example prompts in Appendix B are applied to the MAIB corpus for knowledge extraction. To ensure cross-language consistency, both the English and Chinese corpora are processed under a unified schema and prompt framework. The schema and prompts for the Chinese corpus are directly translated from the English templates and reviewed by bilingual experts. All entity categories, relations, attribute definitions, instruction format, and output structures are maintained identical cross the two languages.

All LLM services are accessed through API calls to Siliconflow. a commercial AI cloud service platform. To ensure the isolated memory contexts and optimize performance, separate generative models are used for knowledge extraction and text reconstruction. A lightweight, nonreasoning model with fast response time and stable output is utilized as KG extractor. In contrast, a reasoning-augmented LLM is used for text reconstruction where its logical inference capabilities are essential for producing plausible content from unordered triplets. The LLMs used in this case along with the default decoding parameters setting is sum marized in Table 3. These generative LLMs and embedding models used are all designed for multilingual and cross-lingual applications. The same models are employed for knowledge extraction across both the English and Chinese corpora (Team Qwen, 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024).

From the MAIB corpus, 3612 entities and 9783 relations are extracted. 1263 entities and 2463 relations are obtained from the MSA corpus. The resulting SPO triplets along with their embeddings and the corresponding original text chunks, are written in a Neo4j graph data base. To support downstream semantic similarity analysis, the vector embeddings are stored as attributes of entities and relations within Neo4j. This approach enables direct use of embeddings for in-graph similarity computations without the need for an external vector data base or plugin. It also simplifies data management and maintains con sistency across symbolic and embedding-based representations. A subgraph visualization based on the MAIB corpus is illustrated in Fig. 3. In the graph structure, each accident-level text chunk is incorporated into the graph as a dedicated “chunk” node. All entities extracted from the same chunk are linked to it via a “source” relation (i.e., <entity, source, chunk>) preserving the contextual integrity of the sub-graphs. The detailed information associated with nodes, including contents, vector embeddings, and enumerated attributes, can be retrieved through Cypher queries.

text: 4.3. Comparative analysis of model performance and metric effectiveness

To validate the feasibility of the LLM-based pipeline and the effec tiveness of the customized modeling metrics, a comparative analysis is conducted between the LLM-based method and widely employed natu ral language processing methods (e.g., BERT-based methods), with both established measures and the proposed indicators.

The comparative analysis is exclusively carried out on the MAIB corpus since the sample size of the MSA dataset is insufficient for reliable model training and validation. Entities and relations are annotated by an advanced LLM (ChatGPT 5) prompted via the same schema described in Appendix A. Two BERT-based models, namely BERT-NER model and BERT-based relation classification model, are trained on 70 % of the dataset, with 10 % reserved for hyperparameter tuning and 20 % for testing (Kenton and Toutanova, 2019). Table 4 summaries the evalua tion results of BERT-based and LLM-based approaches on test set, respectively. Both traditional metrics and the newly proposed metrics consistently demonstrate the superior performance of applying inte grating LLM into schema-based knowledge extraction tasks. Specifically, the substantially higher recall can be attributed to the LLM’s stronger contextual understanding which promotes the identification of valid triplets. Furthermore, the enhanced performance in text reconstruction accuracy indicates that the LLM-based method can preserve the se mantic coherence of the original text more effectively.

This comparative evaluation also highlights the alignment and dif ference between traditional metrics and the proposed evaluation in dicators. While precision, recall, and F1 evaluates the fidelity of the extracted triplets with respect to the original text, the proposed recon struction accuracy serves a complementary role from a global semantic perspective. The consistent performance where the LLM-based method outperforms the BERT-based method by roughly 10 % across these two types of metrics, i.e., macro-average F1 score and mean reconstruction accuracy, indicates the validity of the proposed accuracy metrics as a complementary indicator for assessing extraction quality without relying on manually annotated data. Besides, the proposed accuracy metrics measure the global semantic integrity of the extracted knowl edge rather than solely on triplet-level correctness. Therefore, it is inherently more sensitive to errors since a single incorrect or missing triplet can disrupt the logical consistency or semantic coherence of the whole reconstructed text. In contrast, the complexity metrics evaluate the structural aspects of the developed KG beyond mere extraction ac curacy. Although BERT-based approach obtains satisfactory extraction accuracy in traditional indicators, the developed KG may still exhibit redundant structures and limited interpretability, as reflected by the complexity metrics. The noticeable differences in complexity metrics between two methods highlight the necessity of incorporating structural evaluation.

4.4. Quality assessment of weather-related marine accident knowledge graph

In this section, the LLM-aided KG construction using the default configuration, is evaluated in detail through the proposed evaluation framework. The assessment is performed on both the MAIB and MSA corpora, and the corresponding evaluation results are summarized in Table 5.

Overall, entity redundancy is prevalent in both KGs, whereas the relation redundancy and graph structure complexity remain acceptable. The accuracy indicators suggest that the sub-graphs successfully capture the core semantics of the original accident investigation reports. How ever, the KG developed from the MSA corpus exhibits lower semantic fidelity compared to MAIB corpus, likely due to variations in language structure and narrative style across the two data sources.

A detailed investigation is conducted to explore the errors produced by LLMs during knowledge extraction. All the redundant clusters with a size larger than 3, as well as all the redundant relations, are recorded for investigation. Through a thorough review of the clustered entities and triplets, typical redundancy types for entities and relations are identified and summarized in Table 6 along with the proportions of each type. In English corpus, morphological variants are the main source of redun dant entities, while such issues are absent in the Chinese text. Other redundant entities in the MAIB-based KG mainly stem from inconsistent and vague entity descriptions. In contrast, in the MSA-based KG, syno nyms and paraphrased expressions are more common than especially in event descriptions containing longer and more complex phrases. Across both corpora, multiple relations occur in scenarios such as confusion between ship responses and operations, and misinterpretation of schema-defined temporal (occurredOn) and spatial (occurredAt) re lations. Additionally, frequent occurrence of self-loops in both corpora indicates that LLM hallucinations remains a major source of error in relation extraction.

This section explores how key configuration choices—including schema design, prompt engineering, and LLM decoding parameter s—affect the quality of the generated weather-related marine accident KG. text: 5.2. Impact of schema and prompt design on KG quality

This section discusses the impact of schema and prompt design on the quality of generated KG for marine accident analysis. To systemat ically assess their effects, schema and prompt revisions are implemented in a step-wise manner, with each step introducing incremental modifi cations. This design allows for the exploration of KG quality sensitivity to specific configuration changes and enables the identification of key factors that contribute to KG quality improvements.
5.2.1. KG quality assessment under incremental schema optimizations

The schema is revised by introducing more fine-grained entity and relation types to improve extraction precision and semantic clarity. In the first phase, broad entity categories, such as ContributingFactor, are subdivided into specific types according to their enumerated attributes, e.g., EquipmentFailure, HumanErrors, MaintenanceIssue. Additionally, descriptions are incorporated to guide the KG extractor in accurately aligning extracted entities with schema-defined concepts. In the second phase, the generic cause relation is disaggregated into more nuanced types, including directCauseOf, exacerbates, and resultsIn for better distinction between primary, secondary, and compounding causal links in accident narratives. All experiments are conducted under the default KG extractor parameter setting (temperature is 0.1 and Top-p is 1.0).

Fig. 6 illustrates the results of accuracy and complexity evaluation under incremental schema optimizations. Fig. 6(a) indicates that the schema refinement improves the overall semantic fidelity of the extracted knowledge SPO triplets. Notably, the subdivision of entity types contributes more to similarity score improvements than modifying relation schema. These improvements are particularly significant in cases where semantically central information is previously missed resulting in low similarity between original and reconstructed texts. The gains in accuracy are attributed to the increased semantic granularity and its constraint effect, which collectively enhance entity alignment, reduce ambiguity, and guide the LLM to a narrower and more precise output search space.

Fig. 6(b) shows that while overall KG accuracy gets improved, rela tion redundancy increases and the graph becomes structurally more complex, incorporating additional branches to represent subordinate content. Refining the entity schema into finer-grained types improves the accuracy of the NER sub-task by helping the model better align mentions with their corresponding entity types, reducing errors caused by overly broad schema. In contrast, refining relation types does not yield the desired effect and instead introduces semantic ambiguity and overlap between relations. For example, the relations exacerbates and causes are both assigned between “pitching” and “container stow collapse”. While causes typically indicates that an event leads to the emergence of a new problem, exacerbates implies the intensification of an already existing issue. The model, however, fails to fully distinguish this nuance when presented with a more fine-grained relation schema, resulting in redundant and overlapping relation assignments. Moreover, invalid triplets, such as < crew member died, resultsIn, crew member died>, highlight the model’s inability to detect or prevent self-loops. These results suggest that while schema refinement enhances expres siveness and accuracy, it may also lead to redundant or overlapping relation assignments, especially when contextual or structural con straints (e.g., mutual exclusivity or relation validity) are not explicitly enforced.
5.2.2. KG quality assessment under incremental prompt optimizations

Prompt designs are refined at each stage of the knowledge extractior pipeline to improve the KG quality. In the NER step, the prompt is enhanced with additional instructions emphasizing the completeness of entity detection, clarity and conciseness in naming, and deduplication of semantically identical entities. For entity standardization, illustrative examples are incorporated into the prompt to demonstrate how to unify similar terms into consistent expressions, thereby mitigating the entity redundancy. In the relation extraction step, targeted prompt revisions are introduced to reduce relation redundancy. Specifically, additional prompts are incorporated to help the model identify and avoid two common types of errors: (1) assigning multiple spurious relations to the same pair of entities, and (2) generating self-loop triplets where the subject and object are the same entity. Table 9 summarizes the addi tional prompt instructions applied for each stage of the extraction process.

The evaluation results presented in Fig. 7 reveal trade-offs between semantic accuracy, redundancy control, and core structure preservation. text: 5.3. Domain knowledge-enhanced optimization for maritime safety KG construction

Based on the proposed assessment framework and experimental findings, an iterative optimization process tailored to the characteristics of marine accident KGs is proposed. For each iteration, the process comprises four stages—evaluation, diagnosis, adjustment, and re-eval uation—guided by domain-specific considerations:
(1) Evaluate the developed KG using complexity and accuracy indicators.

(2) Diagnose performance bottlenecks by comparing observed indi cator values with predefined targets, such as redundancy in en tities (e.g., vessel types and weather conditions), misalignment of hazardous event timelines, and omission of key accident causations.
(3) Refine the schema, prompts or decoding parameters based on diagnostic insights
(4) Re-construct and re-evaluate the KG quality to assess improvements.

In Step 1, a quantitative assessment is performed using the indicators proposed in Section 3.5 to assess the current quality of the KG. Step 2 determines the optimization objective for the current iteration by linking evaluation outcomes with specific refinement strategies. Given the inherent trade-off between preserving accuracy and reducing complexity, each iteration typically focuses on improving one dimension at a time. Step 3, the core of the quality optimization process, involves adjusting various configuration components based on diagnostic in sights. The following paragraphs detail specific adjustments tailored to the maritime transport safety domain, with a focus on either reducing the complexity or improving the accuracy.

When the indicators show excessive redundancy or invalid struc tures, configuration adjustments should aim to streamline the graph. For example, schema refinement can draw on taxonomies according to the marine accident reporting standards by subdividing broad entity types, such as MaintenanceIssue, into granular subtypes (e.g., failure not detected, improper repair, inadequate maintenance, and lack of main tenance) each with each with domain-relevant attributes, such as vessel component and status. Entity standardization can be supported by integrating a reference list of canonical marine accident terminology to assist LLMs in merging semantically equivalent entities. During relation extraction, prompts should instruct the model to catch the causal logic common in maritime safety investigations, and to check and filter out invalid SPO triplets. Conservative decoding parameter setting can help control generation variability and reduce noise.

If accuracy is the main concern, optimizations should focus on improving extraction fidelity, particularly around accident causal se quences and timelines. Schema enhancements may include explicitly defining time-sensitive relations like occurredOn, occurredAt, or cause, ensuring proper alignment of events such as engine failure and emer gency response. Slot-filling templates can help ensure all critical acci dent attributes—such as vessel class, incident location, and casualties—are systematically extracted. Prompt refinements should emphasize the expected content (e.g., causes, outcomes) and include timestamp alignment instructions to ensure accurate temporal linking. Experiment results suggest that a more exploratory parameter configu ration may improve the precision of knowledge extraction.

Moreover, additional considerations include the inherent variability of LLM outputs and their sensitivity to schema design. Since LLMs may generate different results across runs, aggregating outputs from multiple generations can yield more stable and robust results. Furthermore, schema sensitivity implies that iterative, fine-grained refinements allow performance impacts to be evaluated incrementally. Analysis of specific low-quality extractions provides valuable feedback for adjusting schema components for specific entity types and relations, enabling a more controlled and resilient optimization process.

Finally, Step 4 involves re-constructing with refined configuration and re-evaluating the KG using the same indicators. This is a critical step for verifying whether the adjustments made in the current iteration effectively address the diagnosed issues. The iterative re-evaluation process ensures steady quality improvements and provides empirical feedback to guide further refinement. Through this closed-loop process, domain knowledge is continuously integrated and validated, enabling the construction of more accurate, compact, and interpretable KGs tailored to marine accident analysis.
5.4. Practical applications and implications

The automated marine KG construction pipeline of marine accident, in conjunction with the evaluation framework, offer practical value for enhancing the data integration, regulatory efficiency, and operational intelligence in maritime safety management.

The LLM-based KG construction pipeline enables maritime author ities to maintain continuously updated knowledge bases. By automati cally extracting causal factors and safety violations from newly issued investigation reports, it extensively reduces the reliance on laborintensive manual review in KG updating. Through transforming large volumes of unstructured marine accident narratives into structured graph model under a predefined schema, quantitative risk assessment on accident reports becomes more feasible. Statistical evaluation of key entities (e.g., weather condition, equipment failures or human factors) and their causal chains over a broader time span can reveal trends of emerging hazards, offering insights for early warning. Moreover, the automated constructed KG enhances knowledge retrieval and reasoning capabilities in operational contexts. By connecting historical accident records with shared nodes, such as vessel characteristics, environmental conditions, and causal mechanisms, a RAG system incorporating such KGs can align ongoing operational states with analogous historical in cidents (Ren et al., 2025). This capability enables real-time decisions for crew members and safety officers, assisting in the identification of po tential risk escalation pathways and the formulation of appropriate mitigation strategies.

The proposed KG quality evaluation framework is fundamental for more reliable real-world applications of KGs in maritime safety man agement. The introduced metrics can help identify redundancy and semantical loss in extracted knowledge prior to KG deployment within safety regulatory or accident investigation systems. The framework forms a quantitative feedback loop, enabling continuous optimization of the schema design, prompt formulation, and model decoding parame ters setting without the need for extensive manual data annotation. Moreover, this evaluation framework provides a robust foundation for benchmarking different KG construction methods and supports the development of standardized and validated KGs for maritime safety analysis and decision support applications.
6. Conclusion

This study has explored the application of LLMs for automated KG construction and assessment within the maritime safety domain. A knowledge extraction pipeline has been proposed, encompassing NER, entity standardization, and relation extraction, with one-shot prompting techniques employed to guide LLM outputs using a predefined schema. To assess the resulting KG, a dual-perspective evaluation framework is developed measuring the semantic fidelity and structural redundancy. The proposed method is applied to weather-related marine accident investigation reports from both the MAIB in the UK and the MSA in China, demonstrating its adaptability across linguistic and narrative variations. Through systematic experiments, the impacts of LLM decoding parameters, schema, and prompts on the LLM-based knowl edge extraction are analyzed. The experiment results reveal inherent trade-offs among semantic accuracy, redundancy control, and core structure preservation. Based on these findings, an iterative optimiza tion framework is proposed, incorporating domain knowledge to refine schema, prompts, and model parameters for improved KG generation in the maritime safety context.

Despite these contributions, several limitations remain. The main issues and corresponding future research directions are summarized as follows. First, while the current knowledge base is limited in weatherrelated scope, extending the framework to a wider range of accident types remains a crucial future direction. Such an extension will increase the complexity of schema design and highlight the trade-off between schema granularity and the LLM’s capability for comprehension. Sec ond, future research could explore the integration of diverse data sources including maritime accident records, deck logs, Automatic Identification System (AIS) data, and communication transcripts. Combining textual, numerical, and sensor-based information may allow the knowledge graph to capture richer representations of vessel behavior and environmental conditions. Moreover, future studies could examine cross-lingual adaptive mechanisms such as multilingual em beddings and schema alignment to improve the transferability and robustness of KG construction in diverse maritime jurisdictions and linguistic contexts
